FROM OUR SPECIAL CORRESPONDENT

NEW YORK, January — In my last letter I threatened to inflict upon your readers a detailed description of the grand skating and fancy dress carnival announced to take place on the next night at Major OSMAN'S Park. True to my promise, my threat duly took my stand in one of the uncomfortably crowded Sixth Avenue cars, in company with a party of ladies and gentlemen, portion of them Charlestonians and the rest from Sumter &c. After jolting about most unpleasantly in the densely packed car, during a ride of nearly three miles, we got out at the corner of Fifty-ninth street and found ourselves at the scene of action. On entering the large enclosure we stand on a highly elevated eminence and look down upon the scene below. The young moon shines brightly, and hundreds of lanterns of the variegated hues of the bow of promise lend their light to the ice. Bengal fires of different colors shine here and there with lurid glare, the light reflected by the snow-white surface of frozen water as if it were with diamonds. So far as the fancy dress portion of the programme was concerned, it was a man who hires out costumes was not on hand as had been promised; nevertheless, we noted among the skaters here and there an Irish Light Red Riding HOOD, a tall lank Yankee, score scores of gentlemen with wax noses and some with masks. The skating itself was a magnificent sight. As our party descended the deep flight of stairs, and noted the graceful evolutions of the skaters, we hastened to get upon advantage, seated on one of the many benches that are placed around the sides of the pond. It is really almost beyond the power of language to give an adequate idea of the beauty of the scene.

Some of the best skaters in this city were present, one lady in particular, who is famous in one of the places on the Central Park Lake last year. To see such a beautiful and graceful woman dance is one of the difficulties to imagine how thoroughly graceful a woman can be when, with swan-like movement she glides along the smooth surface of the ice. The young lady we have mentioned was the observed of all observers, and yet there were scores of skaters both male and female, who were almost equally expert. Now they go round and round in circles, now in conceivable and inconceivable manner—the young lady always surrounded by the largest crowd of admirers, when she shoots off like a tiny silver arrow shot from a magic bow, and with the speed of a startled fawn glides across the pond and is lost to view in the crowd till we see her, again near at hand, and she flies past us with the swiftness of the wind and once again is lost in the crowd.

It was a sight well worth witnessing, and about twenty Charlestonians, for I counted that number on the ice, conspicuous among whom was the good oldness.

There was quite a lively time yesterday among men in general fight. At a meeting of the Board of Councilmen there was general row between the Democratic and Republican members, which threatened to lead to a hand-to-hand engagement: indeed the first shot was actually fired by Mr. Long, who complimented the President by hitting his ink stand at his head, at the same time accusing him of carrying a pistol in direct violation of the law. This was the first and last shot thrown; and, though the meeting broke up in most tremendous disorder, no regular engagement took place.

Benjamin Bethel Beast Butler has three civil duties in leaving New Orleans without settling his debts. Yesterday these actions were transferred from the Supreme Court here to the Supreme Court of the United States, or rather a motion was made to that effect which will probably be granted.

The war between the liquor dealers and the enemy. Last night the liquor men passed resolutions in favor of employing counsel to represent them before the Legislature, and prove to that august body that the prevention of the citizen of this glorious land of freedom from imbibing spirituous liquors is an impossibility. Each one of the brewers, distillers and venders of the enemy will subscribe five dollars in aid of the good cause. Meanwhile liquor and beer will be distilled, brewed, sold and drunk, in spite of the law.

Here she receives religious instruction, is furnished with work, is well clad and comfortably supported, and every inducement to reform is offered. In the past year hundreds of these young women have been reclaimed from the paths of evil, and many of them have been restored to their friends purer in heart, poor creatures than when they were first tempted.

Irvin has left us and set out on her Western tour; she will return in April, and, after playing a short engagement goes to Paris to hold forth there during the Exposition. Edwin Booth will continue to play at the Winter Garden till March.
